title: Cattle and horses

names.gloss: hump, as on a Brahman bull

scientificName: Bos taurus × Bos indicus; Equus caballus

identification.basis: Karma Waters is a working cattle station; the dictionary has words for horses, riders, stockmen, whips and the Brahman's hump, and no word for cattle themselves in the sources used here.

summary: **[yarraman](word:yarraman)** 'horse', **[danda](word:danda)** 'chestnut horse', **[mala-yarraman](word:mala-yarraman)** 'good rider', **[marrkin-marrkin](word:marrkin-marrkin)** 'nickname for a stockman', **[wubun](word:wubun)** 'hump, as on a Brahman bull', **[wuybu](word:wuybu)** 'whip' and **[kubarru](word:kubarru)** 'sound of whip' are the dictionary's station words; there is no word for cattle in it, and that gap is for the contribution box below [ref:hershberger1982]. [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) is a cattle station: 'cattle on Karma Waters are Braham Cross and we run a herd of around 1600 mixed cattle', with 'two rounds of mustering undertaken annually in May and September', 'carried out with 6 to 8 men on horseback and helicopter' [ref:kw-cattle]. The Brahman 'has a high tolerance of heat, sunlight and humidity, and good resistance to parasites' and 'in Australia it is the most numerous breed of cattle'; the station horse is the Australian Stock Horse, 'a hardy breed of horse noted for endurance, agility, and good temperament' [ref:wiki-brahman] [ref:wiki-stock-horse]. Both have been on this river since the Palmer gold rush of 1873 brought stations behind it, and both run wild: the station musters 'feral cattle' out of the river and fences 'to exclude feral bulls', and Queensland 'may have as many as 200,000 feral horses', an animal that 'competes with cattle for food and water' and 'damages creek banks and waterways' [ref:wiki-palmer-river] [ref:kw-outback] [ref:kw-cattle] [ref:qld-feral-horse]. This page is the cattle and horses as things on country: how to read them, how to be safe around them, what the station's rules are, and the long history of Aboriginal people as the stockmen and stockwomen of the north, from the stations that took the waterholes to the Wave Hill walk-off of 1966 and the stolen wages settlement of 2019 [ref:wiki-wave-hill] [ref:wiki-stolen-wages] [ref:kw-induction].

infobox.label: Kuku Yalanji
infobox.value: yarraman (horse); danda (chestnut horse); mala-yarraman (good rider); marrkin-marrkin (stockman); wubun (Brahman's hump); wuybu, kubarru (whip, its crack); karra, ngurran (rope)

infobox.label: On Karma Waters
infobox.value: About 1,600 Brahman-cross cattle in 5 breeder and 8 smaller paddocks; musters in May and September with 6–8 riders and a helicopter; bulls out in September, back in early February

infobox.label: The breed
infobox.value: Brahman: bred in the United States from Indian cattle; in Australia since 1933; over a million in Queensland by 1987; heat- and tick-tolerant

infobox.label: Horses
infobox.value: Australian Stock Horse, recognised as a breed in 1971; feral horses number up to 200,000 in Queensland and are not a restricted animal

infobox.label: Wild ones
infobox.value: Feral bulls and river cattle mustered out; feral horses eat as much as 1–2 cows each and foul waterholes

infobox.label: Rules
infobox.value: Station induction: no weapons or hunting dogs for visitors, gates as found, fire bans, stay out of the yards at muster

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
**[yarraman](word:yarraman)** 'horse' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[danda](word:danda)** 'chestnut horse' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[mala-yarraman](word:mala-yarraman)** 'good rider', built on *mala* as in **[mala-kural](word:mala-kural)** 'good diver' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[marrkin-marrkin](word:marrkin-marrkin)** 'nickname for a stockman', doubled from *marrkin* 'gun' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[wubun](word:wubun)** 'hump, as on a Brahman bull' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[wuybu](word:wuybu)** 'whip (english loan word)', **[kubarru](word:kubarru)** 'sound of whip', and **[dalkil](word:dalkil)** 'to crack a nut or whip, or shoot a gun' [ref:hershberger1982]. **[karra](word:karra)** 'rope, cord, string' and **[ngurran](word:ngurran)** 'rope, also dilly bag made from rope'; **[wukurril](word:wukurril)** 'follow; weave; make a fence; imitate'; **[yamba](word:yamba)** 'house' [ref:hershberger1982].

There is no Kuku Yalanji word for cattle, bullock or beef in the dictionary: the cattle came with the stations and the people who made the dictionary at the Bloomfield used the English words [ref:hershberger1982]. The words the Western Yalanji stock-workers used on the Mitchell and Palmer stations, for cattle, for the camp, for the gear, are the kind of thing the contribution box below is for.

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
**The cattle.** 'Cattle on Karma Waters are Braham Cross', and the Brahman 'is an American breed of zebuine-taurine hybrid beef cattle', 'bred in the United States from 1885 using cattle originating in India'; it 'has a high tolerance of heat, sunlight and humidity, and good resistance to parasites', 'in Australia it is the most numerous breed of cattle', and 'exports of cattle of this breed to Australia began in 1933', so that 'by 1987 there were over a million in Queensland alone' [ref:kw-cattle] [ref:wiki-brahman]. The hump the dictionary names, **[wubun](word:wubun)**, is the Brahman's mark: a fleshy hump over the shoulders, a loose dewlap, long ears and a grey or red coat; a Brahman bull weighs about '887 kg' [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:wiki-brahman]. Cattle 'are large artiodactyls, mammals with cloven hooves', 'like all bovid species, they can have horns, which are unbranched and are not shed annually', 'bulls are larger than cows of the same breed by up to a few hundred kilograms', and 'the gestation period for a cow is about nine months' [ref:wiki-cattle]. They are ruminants: 'cattle have one large stomach with four compartments; the rumen, reticulum, omasum, and abomasum', and a mob at rest in the shade in the heat of the day is chewing the cud [ref:wiki-cattle].

**The horses.** 'The Australian Stock Horse (or Stockhorse), has been especially bred for Australian conditions. It is a hardy breed of horse noted for endurance, agility, and good temperament', 'still valued as a working horse by stockmen and stockwomen throughout Australia', and 'formal recognition of Australian Stock Horses as a distinct breed began in June 1971' [ref:wiki-stock-horse]. The feral horse is the same animal gone wild: 'average size 1–1.6m shoulder height', 'average weight 350–450kg', 'coat colour varies, ranging from bay (brown body with black mane and tail) to chestnut (orange), black, brown and grey', with 'strong legs well adapted to long-distance travel in search of food and water' [ref:qld-feral-horse]. The dictionary's **[danda](word:danda)** is the chestnut [ref:hershberger1982].

**The feral cattle.** 'Fencing the country into large paddocks has cut back on mustering costs, and has improved the quality of cattle by excluding feral bulls'; on the muster film the station's owner is 'running a few feral cattle mainly into portable yard here', because 'cattle get into the river here and they're pretty hard to get out sometimes' [ref:kw-cattle] [ref:kw-outback]. A feral bull is a bull born and grown unbranded in the scrub; it is the most dangerous animal on the station after the [saltwater crocodile](entry:saltwater-crocodile), and the one a walker in the river country is most likely to meet.

sections.heading: Station stock or wild
sections.body:
**Branded or clean.** The station's cattle carry its brand and the National Livestock Identification tag, since 'all livestock leaving property is identified with the NLIS standards'; a grown beast with neither is a cleanskin, and a cleanskin bull is a feral bull, which the fences are there to exclude [ref:kw-cattle]. The weaners 'are taken off during both rounds' and run in their own paddocks, so a mob of small cattle in a river paddock in June is the station's, not strays [ref:kw-cattle].

**Horse or brumby.** A station horse is shod or recently shod, handled and in a paddock near the homestead or at the muster camp; a feral horse is in a small mob with a stallion, unshod and shy, and it 'disrupts station horses during stock mustering (feral stallions may take mares from station stocks and upset breeding programs)' [ref:qld-feral-horse]. 'The feral horse is not a prohibited or restricted invasive animal under the *Biosecurity Act 2014*', unlike the [pig](entry:pigs), the [wild dog](entry:dingo-and-dogs) and the [cat](entry:weeds-and-ferals); it is the station's to manage [ref:qld-feral-horse] [ref:qld-feral-pig].

**Cattle or buffalo.** There are no water buffalo on this river in the sources used here; a big dark animal with swept-back horns wallowing in a lagoon on the lower Mitchell is a question for the Kowanyama rangers, and on the upper river it is a Brahman bull [ref:kw-cattle].

**Tracks.** A cow's track is a cloven print, two toes with a gap, larger and rounder than a [pig's](entry:pigs), which shows the dew claws; a horse's is a single round hoof, the only one on country; the [tracks page](entry:tracks-and-signs) has the native prints beside them [ref:wiki-cattle].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
**Pads and water.** Cattle make pads, the worn single-file tracks that run from the paddocks to the dams and the river gaps, and they foul water: the station 'constructed 45km of fence to exclude stock from the Mitchell River in 1992 and constructed 15 stock dams to compensate for the loss of stock access to the river' [ref:kw-land]. A river pool with cattle sign on the sand, dung, pads cut into the bank and the water muddied, is one where the fence is down, and that is worth telling the station [ref:kw-land]. Feral horses 'degrade soil by overgrazing and trampling, mainly around water holes' and 'damage watering points (particularly during drought), as well as fences' [ref:qld-feral-horse].

**Dung and grazing.** The station runs 'monthly dung tests' and feeds phosphorus 'all year as protein levels are sufficient to allow for weight gains'; dung is also the sign of what is being eaten, and a paddock eaten flat to the stylo is one that is due for spelling, since 'our breeders alternate on a year on year off spelling regime which allows the country to regenerate and maintain our stylos and 3 p grasses' [ref:kw-cattle]. The 'stylos' are the introduced legumes the station seeds; see [weeds and ferals](entry:weeds-and-ferals) [ref:kw-land].

**The helicopter.** In May and September the muster is 'carried out with 6 to 8 men on horseback and helicopter', and the film has 'two choppers on the other side and we've got one chopper on this side'; a helicopter working low over the river country is the sign the muster is on, and the yards and the paddocks being worked are no place to be [ref:kw-cattle] [ref:kw-outback].

**Bones.** Botulism kills cattle in phosphorus-poor country when they chew bones; 'all stock are inoculated for botulism' on Karma Waters, and the licked, scattered bones of a dead beast are the sign of the hunger behind it [ref:kw-cattle]. A carcass is also where the [wild dogs](entry:dingo-and-dogs), [pigs](entry:pigs) and [kites](entry:eagles-and-hawks) gather, and where the baits go down: 'wild dog baiting is carried out on an "as required" basis which usually consists of two programs annually', with strychnine in the wet and 1080 'in the latter part of the year' [ref:kw-land].

sections.heading: The paddocks and the river
sections.body:
'We have developed the Mitchell country into 5 main paddocks for breeders and 8 smaller paddocks for weaners, finishing steers, aged cows and holding our bulls which we take out in September and return to the breeders in early February', 'to eliminate winter calving and maximise calving percentages'; 'during their time out of the herd the bulls are kept in good stylo country to maintain body weight' [ref:kw-cattle]. The property 'is approximately 45000 hectares, made up of shaly or greywacke ridges'; the block north of the St George 'is very hilly country', and the river block 'enjoys a 50 km frontage to the Mitchell River which is where the homestead is situated' [ref:kw-about]. 'Both blocks were bare of infrastructure and cattle' when the family took them in 1989 and 1991, so everything on them, the fences, the dams, the yards, the paddocks, has been built since [ref:kw-about].

The cattle live in the open [woodland](entry:woodland) on the native pastures and the stylos, come to the dams to drink, and camp under the shade trees in the heat; the river is fenced from them and the places they get in are the problem: 'just in the river here cattle get into the river here and they're pretty hard to get out sometimes' [ref:kw-land] [ref:kw-outback]. Feral horses 'can occupy wide range of habitats, although best adapted to open grassy plains', and in Australia they 'inhabit range of habitats, including deserts, semi-desert plains, rocky ranges, tropical savanna grasslands, forests, scrubs' [ref:qld-feral-horse]. The Atlas has 131 records of cattle and 6 of horses within 60 km of the homestead, which says only that nobody records cattle [ref:ala-karma-60].

**The wider country.** A cattle station 'is a large farm', 'each station has a homestead where the property owner or the manager lives', and 'water may be supplied from a river, bores or dams, in conjunction with rainwater tanks'; Karma Waters' neighbours are the stations of the Mitchell, Walsh and Palmer, and the stock routes that once walked cattle to the railhead, 'six miles a day', are the roads [ref:wiki-cattle-station] [ref:wiki-stock-route].

sections.heading: What cattle and horses do to country
sections.body:
**Grass, fire and weeds.** Cattle eat grass, and the station manages the grass with fire and spelling: 'most of our country is burnt on a 3-4 year cycle', 'we use fire to clean up the country or get rid of excessive fuel loads which has been part of land management in this country for thousands of years', and 'we also use fire to control some weeds and introduced stylos when they become too dominant in the pasture make up' [ref:kw-land]. That is the same fire as on the [hunting-with-fire](entry:hunting-with-fire) page, used for a different animal [ref:kw-land]. The weeds the cattle spread and the station fights are 'Rubber Vine, Giant rats tail (one or two plants annually in a known area) Wynn Cassia, Devils Claw and Calatrope'; 'small infestations are hand pulled while larger areas are poisoned' [ref:kw-land].

**Water.** Cattle and horses foul and trample water, which is why the river is fenced; feral horses 'remove native vegetation by grazing and trampling, with flow-on effects to native wildlife' and 'damage creek banks and waterways', and 'a feral horse consumes plant matter comparable to that consumed by 1–2 cows' [ref:kw-land] [ref:qld-feral-horse]. The clean pools that the [turtles](entry:freshwater-turtle), [cherabin](entry:cherabin) and [waterlilies](entry:water-lilies) need are the fenced ones [ref:kw-land].

**Dogs, roos and calves.** 'This routine management of wild dogs has seen a marked decrease in dog bitten calves and a huge increase in kangaroos and wallaroos which don't pose a problem in this country' [ref:kw-land]. The dog baiting that protects the calves is the reason a [hunting dog](entry:dingo-and-dogs) cannot run free on the station, and the kangaroos it has let increase are the ones on the [wallaby](entry:wallaby) page [ref:kw-land] [ref:kw-induction].

**Carbon.** The station 'conducted a field trail with the Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry on carbon emissions', trialling 'practices than can reduce methane emissions from cattle and increase sequestration of soil carbon', and since 2005 has 'been taking photo points twice year; end of year at break of season and post wet season to monitor the ground cover and species' [ref:kw-land].

sections.heading: The station year
sections.body:
The station year runs on the river's: the bulls go 'out in September' and 'return to the breeders in early February', so the calves drop after the wet rather than in the cold; the musters are in 'May and September', when the roads are open and the cattle are on the dams; 'the wet season program' of dog baiting 'is targeted at problem areas using strychnine as it holds up better in the wet conditions', and the big 1080 program 'is usually carried out in the latter part of the year' [ref:kw-cattle] [ref:kw-land]. The aerial-seeded paddocks 'are used to carry weaners through to the storm season and finish off steers for processing' [ref:kw-land]. The photo points are taken at 'break of season', the first storms, and 'post wet season' [ref:kw-land].

Set against the [seasons page](entry:seasons): the wet closes the station and the river to everything; the little rains bring the first muster; the cold is the quiet grazing time, with the bulls out; the hot season is the second muster, the baits, the burning; the storms are the break [ref:kw-cattle] [ref:kw-land] [ref:bom-palmerville]. A native title holder's calendar on the same country fits around those dates: fishing and gathering in the fenced river paddocks any time, hunting arranged with the station outside the musters and the bait programs [ref:kw-induction] [ref:kw-land].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**Beef.** The station's product is cattle for the meatworks, under the Livestock Production Assurance program 'covering food safety, animal welfare and biosecurity', and the killer, the beast killed for the station's own meat, is the station's to give [ref:kw-cattle]. Beef is cooked the way the [cooking-meat](entry:cooking-meat) page describes for kangaroo, and salted and corned in the old station way; the camp cook's fare is on the [damper page](entry:damper-and-camp-cooking) [ref:wiki-stockman].

**Work.** 'A stockman is responsible for the care for livestock and treatment of their injuries and illnesses. This includes feeding, watering, mustering, droving, branding, castrating, ear tagging, weighing, vaccinating livestock and dealing with their predators'; 'a good stockman is aware of livestock behavioural characteristics, and has an awareness of flight zone distances of the livestock being handled', and 'apart from livestock duties a stock person will inspect, maintain and repair fences, gates and yards' [ref:wiki-stockman]. 'Mustering is a long, difficult and sometimes dangerous job, especially on the vast Australian cattle stations of the Top End', done 'on foot, with various vehicles, horses or with aircraft', and 'cattle mustering lends itself more towards the use of horses' [ref:wiki-muster]. That work was Aboriginal work across the north for a century: on the stations people 'take work as stockmen and domestic help', and 'the pastoralists wanted cheap labour, and workers were exploited and abused' [ref:wiki-wave-hill].

**Hides, horn and hair.** Cattle hide, horn and hoof, and horsehair, replaced possum skin and [sinew](entry:sinew) for some jobs on the stations: a greenhide rope, a hair belt, a hide water bag; the dictionary's **[karra](word:karra)** 'rope, cord, string' covers them all [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1904].

**The whip.** 'The sound of whip', **[kubarru](word:kubarru)**, is the muster's sound; a stockwhip is plaited from kangaroo hide or redhide on a cane handle, and the [string page](entry:string-and-twine) has the plaiting [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:roth1904].

sections.heading: Living with cattle and horses on the station
sections.body:
**The station's rules come first.** The induction form every visitor signs says 'weapons and hunting dogs are not allowed', gates are left as found, fires only where and when the station says, and the muster, the yards and the baits are out of bounds; native title holders arrange their own hunting with the station, and the [law page](entry:law-hunting-and-fishing) has the native title side [ref:kw-induction] [ref:kw-land] [ref:alrc].

**Walking through cattle.** Walk, do not run; talk so they know where you are; give a cow with a calf and any bull a wide berth; never get between a beast and the gap it wants; if a bull turns to face you with its head down, back off slowly toward a tree or a fence [ref:wiki-stockman]. The 'flight zone' is the distance at which an animal moves off; stay outside it and the mob walks away from you, inside it and the mob can go anywhere [ref:wiki-stockman].

**Around horses.** Approach from the front quarter where the horse can see you, speak, hand flat; never walk close behind; a feral mob is left alone, since a stallion defends his mares and 'ground shooting is discouraged because it is difficult to follow up on any wounded horses' [ref:qld-feral-horse].

**Riding.** The horses are the station's; a rider who wants to learn the station's work asks the station. The old way of learning was the camp: 'in these areas the days in the saddle are often very long as the cattle have to be mustered and then driven to yards or a paddock where they can be held', 'sleeping in a swag (bedroll) on the ground with limited food choices' [ref:wiki-stockman] [ref:wiki-swag].

**Gates and fences.** 'Fencing the country into large paddocks' is the station's whole system; a gate left open mixes the bulls with the breeders or lets the weaners into the river, and a cut fence lets cattle into the fenced pools; leave every gate as you found it and report a fence down [ref:kw-cattle] [ref:kw-land].

**Feral cattle and horses.** They are the station's to muster or shoot; a cleanskin in the river is 'pretty hard to get out', and it is not a hunting target for a visitor under the induction [ref:kw-outback] [ref:kw-induction]. Feral horses 'may be trapped in trap yards or mustered', and 'aerial shooting can be a humane control method when carried out by skilled shooters' [ref:qld-feral-horse].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
**Bulls and cows with calves.** A Brahman bull weighs near 900 kg; a feral bull in the river scrub is the most dangerous land animal on the station [ref:wiki-brahman] [ref:kw-outback]. Keep a tree between you and a bull, never a fence you cannot get through, and never go into the yards during a muster [ref:wiki-stockman].

**Horses.** Kicks, bites and falls are the stockman's injuries; a horse kicks backward and sideways, so stand at the shoulder [ref:wiki-stockman].

**Disease.** Cattle carry nothing a walker catches in passing, but the feral animals that live with them do: the [pig page](entry:pigs) has brucellosis and leptospirosis, 'wild dogs' carry hydatids, and the cattle tick is the reason the Brahman was brought in [ref:nsw-brucellosis] [ref:qld-wild-dog] [ref:wiki-brahman]. Wash after handling any carcass; a station killer is dressed clean on a rail, not on the ground [ref:nsw-brucellosis].

**Baits.** The 1080 and strychnine baits laid for wild dogs kill any dog that finds them; 'the second program is usually carried out in the latter part of the year and covers a much larger area' [ref:kw-land]. No dog on the station without the station's say, and no touching a bait or a baited carcass [ref:kw-induction] [ref:kw-land].

**Vehicles.** Cattle on the road at night, and feral horses that 'pose danger to drivers on some roads', are the commonest station accident; drive slowly at dusk and dawn [ref:qld-feral-horse].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
**The history.** Cattle came to this river behind the gold: William Hann 'found gold in a sandy bed of the river in 1872', the Palmer rush began in 1873, the track from Cooktown was cut by an expedition that 'shot a lot' and 'hunted' Aboriginal people 'along the way at the Normanby River, Kennedy River, Kavanaugh Creek, St George River and at Battle Camp', and the stations followed the diggers [ref:wiki-palmer-river]. Across the north the same story ran: Aboriginal peoples 'found their waterholes and soakages fenced off or fouled by cattle', suffered 'lethal reprisals for any attempt to eat the cattle', and 'there was little choice to stay alive but to move onto the cattle stations, receive rations, adopt a more sedentary life and, where possible, take work as stockmen and domestic help' [ref:wiki-wave-hill]. 'Under the system of Aboriginal Protection Boards established by state and federal legislation, Indigenous Australian workers' wages were paid into government-owned trust accounts', 'their access to the bank accounts was severely restricted and in some cases governments illegally expropriated the trust funds', and 'employers frequently underpaid Indigenous workers or made illegal withholdings' [ref:wiki-stolen-wages]. The Queensland class action for 'work done from 1939 to 1972 by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Queensland' 'represented about 10,000 Aboriginal Queenslanders' and 'was settled in July 2019 with a payout of A$190,000,000', 'the biggest ever payout to Indigenous Australians' outside native title [ref:wiki-stolen-wages]. The Wave Hill walk-off of 1966, 'a walk-off and strike by 200 Gurindji stockmen, house servants and their families', 'led by Gurindji man Vincent Lingiari', became 'a key moment in the movement for Aboriginal land rights in Australia' [ref:wiki-wave-hill].

**This station.** The Western Yalanji determination over Karma Waters in 1998 was 'the first consent determination of native title over a pastoral property in Australia', and in the station's words 'this agreement was the first on pastoral lands in Australia negotiated with the Traditional Owners Western Yalanji in good faith even though it took 7 years to complete' [ref:wyac2020] [ref:kw-about]. Native title and the pastoral lease run together on the same paddocks; the Western Yalanji land use plan of 2020 sets out the holders' own aims for the country, and the station's land management is the other half of the same ground [ref:wyac2020] [ref:kw-land]. The stockmen and stockwomen who worked the Mitchell stations, which families, which years, which camps, are a history the contribution box below is for.
